newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Opposition takes over Serbian city.
newsitem.headline: Opposition takes over Serbian city.

text.p: Serbia's opposition bloc took control in the major city of Nis on Monday but its joy was tempered by the difficulties it must conquer before republic-wide elections late in the year.

"The number of tasks you face is enormous, your responsibility is enormous but your enthusiasm is enormous too," Zajedno (Together) coalition co-leader Zoran Djindjic told the inaugural session of the new Nis assembly.

Zajedno won a big majority in November municipal elections, toppling leftists who had ruled the second largest Serbian city since 1945. But its victory was annulled there and in 13 other major towns by the ruling Socialists (SPS).
The move prompted mass street protests which have been held across Serbia for 10 straight weeks.
SPS claims of election irregularities were turned down by a factfinding mission of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).

After exhausting all forms of legal manoeuvring, the SPS finally conceded defeat in Nis, a southern industrial city of 300,000 people. But the former mayor and all new SPS deputies boycotted the new assembly session.
"It's very encouraging to see a peaceful transition of power in Nis, but disappointing that the SPS felt it necessary to boycott," said a Western diplomat on hand for the Zajedno takeover.
"We will not be satisfied until similar respect for the democratic process is shown in all cities mentioned in the OSCE report," he told Reuters.
Hundreds of Nis residents welcome the transfer of authority with whoops of joy and a din of whistles and trumpets that have become the trademark of Zajedno's pro-democracy campaign.

But the mood of jubilation was dampened by the stark reality that Serbian regional governments can achieve little without the patronage of central authorities, which are exclusively in Socialist hands.

Vuk Draskovic, head of the Serbian Renewal Movement (SPO), a member of Zajedno, said in a sober letter to the new assembly that the Socialists would try to split the SPO from its Democratic Party partners.
"The regime will do everything to compromise the new authority and cause a rift between the SPO and Democratic Party," he said.
The DS and SPO are coalition allies in Zajedno with the Civic Alliance.
Draskovic was worried about the empty coffers of Nis as well as the city's decaying infrastructure and the few powers remaining to the municipal administration.
"The regime will introduce all forms of economic and propaganda sanctions against the new authorities," he warned.
"We do expect to find a sorry state in the city coffers. And there is almost no self-rule now in Serbia. Everything is controlled by the (central) state," new Mayor Zoran Zivkovic told Reuters.
"What we are in charge of is the waterworks, sewerage and garbage disposal. Our biggest problem is the economy which is under complete control of republican bodies."
Zajedno does not even have power over the police in Nis, who report to Milosevic's interior ministry in Belgrade. The electricity network is also under control of the Serbian government.
Many state-managed companies in Nis have had their headquarters transferred to places safely under the SPS thumb.
In effect, Serbian cities must depend on infusions of money from the republic government.
"This leaves Zajedno extremely exposed to the whim of the SPS and criticism by the state media," another Western envoy said.
"Without foreign aid to boost the local economy and infrastructure and make life better, Zajedno's own voters will turn away from them at the next elections."

The only big thing going for Zajedno in Nis is the fact that local media have not been summarily absorbed by the state RTS television network as they were in nearby Kragujevac after Zajedno won that city.

"With two independent stations and local television not under the SPS boot, we are probably the most open city in Serbia. We will tell our citizens the truth and hope they will understand the problems we are facing," said Zivkovic.

Western diplomats say they believe the elections were not so much a fight for who will will rule cities but a battle for control of electronic media, Milosevic's most powerful tool in retaining power despite a ravaged economy.
